alalal-e76567-d1e101.summary: Rubric of Article 1: in what genus is the virtue of faith.

alalal-e76567-d1e110.summary: Notes that many questions arise in the text, but two come before it, the first being the genus of the virtue of faith.

alalal-e76567-d1e119.summary: The second preliminary question: whether faith is a virtue.

alalal-e76567-d1e124.summary: First argument that faith is in the genus of knowledge: all speculation of truth belongs to science, which perfects the intellect in speculating truth, and faith sees truth through a mirror in an enigma, which is a kind of speculation.

alalal-e76567-d1e151.summary: Second argument from Hugh of Saint Victor: faith is assent to first truth set below understanding and above opinion; the extremes are in the genus of knowledge, so the mean is too.

alalal-e76567-d1e174.summary: Third argument: the Philosopher says opinion aided by reasons becomes faith, so faith is in the same genus as opinion, a kind of knowledge.

alalal-e76567-d1e187.summary: Similarly, Boethius says an argument is a reason producing faith in a doubtful matter, and what argument produces is in the genus of knowledge.

alalal-e76567-d1e200.summary: Fourth argument: faith comes from hearing (Romans 10:17), and Gregory says God gives understanding when he enlightens the mind about what is heard; that illumination is in the genus of knowledge, so faith too.

alalal-e76567-d1e229.summary: Sed contra: nothing opposed to a vice is knowledge; faith is opposed to the vice of unbelief, a contrary habit, whereas knowledge is opposed only to ignorance as privation.

alalal-e76567-d1e258.summary: Second sed contra: knowledge is of principles evident in themselves or of conclusions proved by reasons; the credible is neither, being above reason, as the Trinity, and Gregory says faith has no merit where reason gives proof; so faith is not knowledge.

alalal-e76567-d1e303.summary: Solution: faith is not in the genus of knowledge. Though it involves cognition, this arises more from affect than from reason, since one can believe only willingly (Augustine). The intellect relates to the will antecedently with things whose evidence compels assent, and consequently with things not evident, to which it assents only because the will freely wills; faith concerns the latter. Hence the masters say that in faith cognition is material and affection formal.
claims: Faith is not a kind of knowledge, since its assent is caused by the will rather than by evidence.
In faith, cognition is the material element and affection the formal element.

alalal-e76567-d1e352.summary: Reply to the first argument: not all speculation of truth is knowledge, only that in which what perfects knowledge formally is present, a proving middle term or a truth seen as true. Faith is knowledge only as practical knowledge is, mixed with affect, which dominates and informs it.

alalal-e76567-d1e383.summary: Reply to Hugh: by knowledge of truth he means face-to-face vision, and by opinion those matters of Scripture one may doubt without danger. Faith is not simply in the genus of knowledge: the one who knows assents to what he sees, the one who opines fears the contrary, the believer assents without seeing the reason for assent.
claims: The believer assents firmly without seeing the reason for assent, unlike the knower and the opiner.

alalal-e76567-d1e416.summary: Reply to Aristotle and Boethius: 'faith' has many senses: truthfulness in promises (God is faithful), certainty of a conclusion from argument (Aristotle's opinion aided by reasons and Boethius' argument producing faith), loyalty among people, confidence of a secure conscience (Romans 14:23), and confidence in works (the farmer sows in faith). Here faith means only assent to first truth in articles not evident to reason.
claims: In theology, faith means assent to first truth in articles not evident to reason.
concepts: faith as assent to first truth

alalal-e76567-d1e497.summary: Reply on hearing: 'hearing' broadly means whatever leads to faith, such as hearing the word and seeing miracles. These do not cause assent but only prompt thought about the credible; since they do not prove sufficiently, they serve faith only on its material side, a slender cognition, while faith is formally perfected by affect.
claims: Preaching and miracles prompt consideration of the credible but do not cause the assent of faith.

alalal-e76567.summary: Article 1 of Distinction 23 asks in what genus faith belongs, and whether it is a form of knowledge. Arguments from faith's seeing in a mirror, from Hugh's definition placing faith between knowledge and opinion, from Aristotle and Boethius, and from faith coming by hearing suggest that it is. Against this, faith is opposed to the vice of unbelief and its objects are neither self-evident nor demonstrable. Albert holds that faith is not in the genus of knowledge. Its assent is caused by the will consenting to what is not evident, so in faith cognition is material and affection formal. The believer assents firmly without seeing the reason, unlike the knower and the opiner. 'Faith' has many senses, but theologically it is assent to first truth in articles not evident to reason. Hearing and miracles prompt consideration but do not cause that assent.
claims: Faith is not a species of knowledge, since its assent is caused by the will rather than by evidence.
In faith, cognition is material and affection formal.
The believer assents firmly without seeing the reason for assent.
External motives such as preaching and miracles prompt belief but do not cause the assent of faith.
